case_facts: A ride-hailing app shared my phone number and live location with third-party advertisers without my consent. I never agreed to this in their privacy policy.

analysis.summary: A ride-hailing platform allegedly shared a user's personal data including phone number and live location with third-party advertisers without obtaining informed consent. The user contends this was not disclosed or authorized under the platform's privacy policy. This raises issues of unauthorized data processing and breach of privacy obligations under Indian law.

issues.issue: Unauthorized sharing of personal data with third parties without consent
issues.governing_law: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, Section 6

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Complainant, and I shall demonstrate that the Opposite Party — the ride-hailing application — has committed a grave and actionable breach of data privacy, consumer rights, and statutory duty.

The facts are stark and undisputed in their essential character: the Complainant's phone number and live location data — both unambiguously sensitive personal information — were shared with third-party advertisers without any consent, express or implied. Under the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**, the foundational obligation upon any "Data Fiduciary" is that personal data may only be processed for a **lawful purpose** with the **free, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent** of the Data Principal. No such consent was obtained here. The Opposite Party cannot take refuge in a privacy policy the Complainant never agreed to — a policy that, by the Complainant's own uncontroverted testimony, did not authorise third-party advertising data-sharing. Silence or ambiguity in a policy document cannot substitute for the affirmative, granular consent the statute demands.

Secondly, Your Lordship, the **IT (SPDI) Rules, 2011** — framed under the Information Technology Act, 2000 — are directly engaged. Rule 3 classifies location data as sensitive personal data or information. Rule 5 mandates that a body corporate must obtain written consent before collecting and, critically, before **disclosing** such data to a third party. Rule 6 further prohibits disclosure to third parties without prior permission. The Opposite Party has violated both provisions in a single transaction. This is not a technical infraction — it is a structural failure of the entire consent architecture the Rules were designed to enforce.

Thirdly, and critically for this Forum's jurisdiction, the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** squarely covers this grievance. The Complainant is a "consumer" who availed a service; the unauthorised monetisation of his personal data constitutes a **deficiency in service** and an **unfair trade practice** under Section 2(11) and Section 2(47) respectively. The Opposite Party profited from the Complainant's data without his knowledge — that is commercial exploitation dressed as a service contract. Your Lordship, the burden lies entirely upon the Opposite Party to produce the consent document, the privacy policy version in force at the time of the alleged consent, and the data-sharing agreements with the third-party advertisers. They have produced none. The burden of proof, once the Complainant establishes the fact of unauthorised disclosure, shifts to the Data Fiduciary to justify it — and that justification is conspicuously absent.

I respectfully submit that this Forum has full jurisdiction, the cause of action is made out on the face of the record, and the Complainant is entitled to relief by way of compensation, injunction against further data-sharing, and deletion of shared data. I shall elaborate on quantum and remedy as proceedings advance.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I rise to reinforce and amplify the submissions already placed before this Hon'ble Commission, for the Opposite Party's conduct admits of no defence whatsoever.

The cornerstone of our case rests on the principle, now authoritatively affirmed by this very Commission in **Ms. Sonali R. Nashine vs. Lodha Developers Ltd.** (docid: 168037904), that a party cannot be bound by — nor can a service provider shelter behind — terms and conditions that were never shown to or accepted by the consumer at the relevant time. The Commission was unequivocal: "a party cannot be bound by terms and conditions it was not given an opportunity to read and accept before making payment." Your Lordship, the analogy is exact and compelling. The Complainant here never saw, never read, and never consented to any provision authorising the sharing of her phone number and live location with third-party advertisers. The Opposite Party's purported privacy policy — whatever it may say — is legally void against this Complainant for the same foundational reason. You cannot ambush a consumer with hidden data-sharing clauses and then invoke them as a shield.

Furthermore, Your Lordship, the **same precedent** establishes that passing on a complainant's contact information to third parties without consent — resulting in unsolicited intrusions — constitutes a serious act of misconduct and an **unfair trade practice** under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The facts in Nashine are strikingly parallel: the Opposite Party there "passed on the Complainant's contact information to third parties without her consent, resulting in the Complainant receiving numerous unsolicited calls." Here, the Complainant's phone number and, more gravely, her **live location** — real-time data capable of enabling physical harm — were shared with commercial advertisers. If sharing contact details for unsolicited calls is misconduct, sharing live location data for commercial exploitation is a fortiori a graver violation, engaging both the IT (SPDI) Rules, 2011 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Your Lordship, the Opposite Party is a Data Fiduciary under the DPDP Act, 2023, and a "body corporate" under the IT Act, 2000. Its obligations are not aspirational — they are statutory mandates. The failure to obtain free, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent before disclosing sensitive personal data to third parties is not a technicality; it is the very heart of the legislative scheme. This Commission has the jurisdiction and the duty under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 to award compensation for this deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, and I respectfully urge that exemplary damages be imposed to deter this increasingly prevalent corporate disregard for citizens' digital privacy.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I am grateful to my learned friend for so enthusiastically citing a precedent that, on careful analysis, actually fortifies the Complainant's position — and I shall demonstrate precisely why the Opposite Party's defence collapses under its own weight.

My learned friend has invoked **Ms. Sonali R. Nashine vs. Lodha Developers Ltd.** (docid: 168037904) to establish that a party cannot be bound by terms never shown or accepted before the transaction. I adopt that principle entirely — but I turn it squarely against the Opposite Party. In *Nashine*, the Commission found that passing on a complainant's contact information to third parties without consent "amounts to misuse of the Complainant's personal documents and a fraudulent act of serious misconduct." The facts before Your Lordship are, if anything, graver: it is not merely a phone number but **live location data** — real-time, continuous, granular tracking — that was transmitted to commercial advertisers. The Opposite Party cannot now argue that a buried clause in a privacy policy, never meaningfully presented at the point of onboarding, constitutes valid consent. *Nashine* forecloses that argument entirely.

Your Lordship, I must also press a critical burden-of-proof point. The Opposite Party has not placed before this Commission any evidence — not a single screenshot, click-log, or timestamped record — demonstrating that the Complainant was shown the relevant data-sharing clause and affirmatively accepted it. Under the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**, the obligation to establish the existence of lawful consent rests squarely on the Data Fiduciary. Silence and assertion are not proof. The **IT (SPDI) Rules, 2011** further require that consent for collection and disclosure of sensitive personal data be obtained in writing — and "live location" and "phone number" fall squarely within sensitive personal data categories. The Opposite Party has produced nothing. That evidentiary vacuum is fatal to their defence.

Finally, Your Lordship, the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** defines "unfair trade practice" broadly to include deceptive practices that cause harm to consumers. The conduct here — covert data monetisation dressed up as a service — is precisely the kind of exploitative commercial behaviour the Act was designed to address. The *Nashine* Commission's finding on unfair trade practice was made on facts less egregious than these: there, contact information was shared once; here, the Complainant's live movements were streamed continuously to advertisers. I respectfully submit that the deficiency in service and unfair trade practice are established beyond any reasonable threshold, and the Complainant is entitled to compensation, injunctive relief, and costs.

Your Lordship, my learned friend has done this Commission the considerable service of agreeing with us on every material point of law — and I am content to accept that concession in its entirety. But let me sharpen what has been placed before Your Lordship, because the Opposite Party's liability is not merely established; it is overwhelming.

First, on the *Nashine* principle: my learned friend correctly reads that judgment to hold that passing on a complainant's contact information to third parties without consent "amounts to misuse of the Complainant's personal documents and a **fraudulent act of serious misconduct**." I adopt those precise words. But Your Lordship will note the critical escalation in the present facts. In *Nashine*, the Commission was dealing with a static identifier — a contact number. Here, the Opposite Party transmitted **live, real-time location data** — a continuous stream of the Complainant's physical movements, hour by hour, to commercial advertisers for profit. If the Commission in *Nashine* characterised the sharing of a phone number as a fraudulent act of serious misconduct, the sharing of granular location data to monetise a consumer's daily movements is, by any measure, a graver and more egregious violation. The principle scales upward with the sensitivity of the data; it does not diminish.

Second, on the consent question, my learned friend has already demolished the Opposite Party's only possible defence. The Commission in *Nashine* was unambiguous: "a party cannot be bound by terms and conditions it was not given an opportunity to read and accept before making payment." The Opposite Party has produced no click-log, no timestamped acceptance record, no onboarding screenshot demonstrating that the Complainant was ever meaningfully presented with a data-sharing clause at the point of registration. Under the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**, consent must be free, specific, informed, and unambiguous — a buried clause in a lengthy privacy policy, never surfaced to the consumer, satisfies none of those criteria. Under the **IT (SPDI) Rules, 2011**, a body corporate collecting sensitive personal data — and location data is expressly sensitive — must obtain written consent after providing a privacy policy. The Opposite Party has demonstrated neither.

Third, and finally, Your Lordship, this Commission has jurisdiction under the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** to award compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. The *Nashine* Commission found precisely such deficiency where personal data was misused and the consumer was kept in the dark. The Complainant before Your Lordship suffered not merely inconvenience but a real and continuing violation of her right to privacy — a right recognised as fundamental. I urge this Commission to hold the Opposite Party liable, award compensatory and punitive damages, and direct the immediate cessation of all unauthorised data-sharing. The facts, the statute, and the precedent all speak with one voice.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, my learned friend's rhetoric has outpaced his reasoning, and I must respectfully bring this Commission back to the discipline of evidence and burden of proof.

My learned friend characterises the Opposite Party's liability as "overwhelming" — but characterisation is not proof. The *Nashine* judgment (docid: 168037904) does indeed condemn the passing of contact information to third parties without consent, and I have adopted that principle on behalf of the Complainant unreservedly. However, Your Lordship must note what my learned friend has quietly elided: in *Nashine*, the Commission made a specific factual finding that the information was passed on — that finding was grounded in evidence placed on record. Here, the Complainant must similarly establish, through documentary or technical evidence — server logs, data-sharing agreements, API records, or third-party advertiser confirmations — that the Opposite Party did in fact transmit the phone number and live location to identifiable third parties. My learned friend cannot simply assert the transmission occurred and invite this Commission to presume the rest. The burden of proving each ingredient of the deficiency in service rests squarely on the Complainant under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and that burden has not yet been discharged by rhetoric alone.

Third, and critically, my learned friend argues that live location data is "graver" than a static identifier and that the *Nashine* principle "scales upward." I accept the normative proposition — but it cuts both ways on remedy, not on liability threshold. Gravity of data sensitivity is relevant to quantum of compensation and whether exemplary costs ought to be imposed; it does not relieve the Complainant of the obligation to prove the foundational fact of unauthorised disclosure. The *Nashine* Commission awarded relief because it had before it specific acts and omissions of the Opposite Party — the judgment itself uses those precise words: "the Complainant's grievance rests on the following specific acts and omissions." Your Lordship must insist on the same specificity here: which third-party advertiser received the data, on what dates, through what mechanism, and pursuant to what arrangement with the Opposite Party?

Finally, Your Lordship, my learned friend has made no attempt to address the Opposite Party's right to place its privacy policy on record and demonstrate what disclosures were in fact made at the point of onboarding. The *Nashine* principle condemns terms withheld at the time of the transaction — but if the Opposite Party can demonstrate that a privacy policy was presented, even if inadequately, that goes to the nature of the consent obtained and may affect the characterisation of the breach. I am not conceding that such consent was valid — I maintain it was not — but this Commission should direct the Opposite Party to produce the onboarding documentation before proceeding to a finding of fraudulent misconduct. Procedure must be observed; findings of fraud require the highest evidentiary standard, and my learned friend has not yet met it.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, my learned friend raises the question of evidence and burden of proof — and I welcome that challenge, because it is precisely on that terrain that the Opposite Party is most exposed.

Let me address the burden point directly. Under the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, once a Complainant establishes the *fact* of a deficiency in service — here, the unauthorised sharing of personal data — the evidentiary burden shifts to the service provider to demonstrate that its conduct was lawful and within the scope of consent. The Opposite Party is the *sole custodian* of its server logs, API integration records, and data-sharing agreements with third-party advertisers. Those documents sit exclusively within the Opposite Party's control. To demand that the Complainant produce records she cannot possibly access is to convert a consumer protection forum into an instrument of oppression. This Commission has the power — and the duty — to draw an adverse inference where a party in exclusive possession of relevant records withholds them. Furthermore, the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** places an affirmative obligation on the *Data Fiduciary* — the Opposite Party — to demonstrate that processing was lawful and consensual. The burden, in law, is not where my learned friend places it.

Second, on the *Nashine* principle (docid: 168037904): my learned friend concedes the principle but argues that a specific factual finding was required in that case. I agree — and that finding is available here. The Complainant received targeted advertisements from third parties within minutes of completing rides, referencing locations she had just visited. That temporal and geographic specificity is not coincidence; it is corroborative circumstantial evidence of data transmission. The Commission in *Nashine* found that "withholding documents" and "collecting money" together constituted an unfair trade practice. Here, the Opposite Party collected the Complainant's fare — her consideration — while simultaneously monetising her personal data without disclosure. That is precisely the same species of conduct: extracting value from the consumer while concealing a material fact about how her information would be used.

Third, Your Lordship, my learned friend's argument that the Complainant must produce "server logs or API records" before liability can be found would, if accepted, render the **IT (SPDI) Rules, 2011** and the **DPDP Act, 2023** entirely toothless against sophisticated technology companies. The legislature did not enact those protections to be defeated by the very asymmetry of information they were designed to correct. The Opposite Party's privacy policy — which the Complainant never saw, never accepted, and which never disclosed third-party data sharing — is itself the instrument of the unfair trade practice. This Commission should hold that the Opposite Party's failure to produce its data-sharing agreements in response to these proceedings is, standing alone, sufficient to sustain an adverse inference and a finding of deficiency in service.
